title: Marriage, Children, Wealth, and the Ransom for Many
summary: On the road south toward Jerusalem Jesus answers a question about divorce by pointing back to creation, blesses little children, and tells a rich man who has kept the commandments to sell everything and follow him. He predicts his death a third time, and when James and John ask for places of honor he teaches that greatness means service, because the Son of Man came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many. At Jericho he restores the sight of blind Bartimaeus, who follows him on the road.
story:
Jesus has now left Galilee for good. The chapter follows him into Judea and the region beyond the Jordan, and then to Jericho, the last town before the climb to Jerusalem. It completes the central section of Mark (8:27 to 10:52), which began just after a blind man was healed in two stages at Bethsaida (8:22-26) and ends with a blind man who sees at once and follows Jesus on the road. Between those two healings Jesus has predicted his death three times, and each time the disciples have misunderstood: Peter rebuked him (8:32), the Twelve argued about who was greatest (9:34), and here, right after the most detailed prediction of all, two of the inner circle ask for thrones.

The chapter is also a walk through a household. Jesus speaks about husbands and wives (verses 2 to 12), children (13 to 16), property and inheritance (17 to 31), and the ranks of servant and slave (42 to 44), the ordinary structures of ancient life, and in each he measures them by the kingdom of God rather than by the custom of the day. Verse 45 then gives the reason behind all of it and the meaning of everything that is about to happen in Jerusalem: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
historical:
The region ‘beyond the Jordan’ (verse 1) was Perea, a strip of land east of the river that belonged, with Galilee, to Herod Antipas, tetrarch from 4 BC to AD 39. Josephus says Antipas held John the Baptist at his Perean fortress of Machaerus and executed him there (Antiquities 18.116-119), and Mark has already told how John died for condemning Antipas's marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife (6:17-18). Josephus adds a detail that sharpens Mark's story: Herodias had divorced her first husband while he was alive, which Josephus calls a flouting of the ancestral laws (Antiquities 18.136). A question about divorce asked in Antipas's land was therefore not idle. Jesus' answer, with its line about a woman who divorces her husband and marries another (verse 12), could be heard as a comment on the ruling house.

The Pharisees' question sat inside a live debate. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 assumed that a man might divorce his wife if he found in her ‘some indecency’ (Hebrew ervat davar), and required him to give her a written certificate. The Mishnah records how the schools of two first-century teachers read the phrase (m. Gittin 9:10): the house of Shammai allowed divorce only for sexual unfaithfulness, the house of Hillel even if she spoiled his cooking, and Rabbi Akiva, a generation after Jesus, even if the husband found another woman more beautiful. Josephus, who divorced his own wife because he was displeased with her conduct (Life 426), paraphrases the law as permitting divorce for any cause (Antiquities 4.253). Some Jewish groups were stricter. The Damascus Document from the Dead Sea community cites ‘male and female he created them’ (Genesis 1:27) against taking a second wife in a man's lifetime (CD 4:20-21), and the Temple Scroll forbids the king to take another wife while the first lives (11QTemple 57:17-19). Jesus' answer sits closest to these strict voices, but he grounds it not in a rule for the king or the community but in creation itself.

Roman law differed from Jewish law. Under Roman law either spouse could end a marriage, and divorce among the Roman upper classes was common. In Jewish law only the husband could issue a divorce; the Mishnah states the principle that a woman may be divorced with or without her consent, but a man divorces only by his own will (m. Yevamot 14:1). Josephus notes it as a breach of Jewish law when Herod's sister Salome sent her husband Costobarus a bill of divorce (Antiquities 15.259-260). Verse 12, which speaks of a woman who divorces her husband, therefore addresses a world where Roman practice and the conduct of the Herodian women had made the wife's divorce a reality, and Mark's readers, probably in the Roman world, lived there.

Jericho, where the chapter ends, was an oasis city in the Jordan valley about 250 meters (825 feet) below sea level, famous for its date palms and balsam groves. Herod the Great built winter palaces there, excavated at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq by Ehud Netzer from the 1970s, and he died at Jericho, probably in 4 BC. New Testament Jericho lay about 2 kilometers south of the ancient mound of Old Testament Jericho. From it a steep road of about 25 kilometers (15 miles) climbed roughly a thousand meters to Jerusalem. Galilean pilgrims had two routes to the feasts: Josephus says it was their custom to pass through Samaria (Antiquities 20.118), while others followed the Jordan valley and came up from Jericho, as Jesus does here. The crowd around him (verse 46) was likely made up partly of pilgrims going up for Passover. The prediction that the Son of Man would be handed over to the Gentiles (verse 33) points to Roman involvement, since the Jewish council probably could not carry out a death sentence on its own authority under Roman rule (compare John 18:31), and crucifixion was a Roman penalty.
cultural:
Marriage in first-century Judaism was arranged between families, often when the bride was young, and it was a legal and economic contract as much as a personal bond. The husband's divorce was a private act that needed no court: he wrote or had written a bill of divorce and handed it to his wife. The Mishnah gives its essential words, ‘behold, you are permitted to any man’ (m. Gittin 9:3), which shows its purpose: to release the woman so that she could marry again without being accused of adultery. A divorced woman usually lost her household and had to return to her father's house or remarry, and she received the sum pledged in her marriage contract (the ketubbah), which was meant to discourage hasty divorce. The Babylonian Talmud ends its tractate on divorce with Rabbi Eleazar's saying that the altar itself sheds tears over a man who divorces the wife of his youth (b. Gittin 90b, drawing on Malachi 2:13-16). Jewish tradition also grieved divorce even as it regulated it.

Adultery in Jewish law was defined by the woman's status: a married woman who slept with another man, or a man who slept with another man's wife, committed adultery against her husband. A married man who slept with an unmarried woman did not commit adultery in the legal sense. Jesus' phrase ‘commits adultery against her’ (verse 11) therefore makes the husband answerable to his own wife, which was new.

Children in the ancient world were loved, but they had no legal standing and could offer nothing in return for attention. Jewish teachers blessed children, and parents might bring them to a respected teacher for a blessing, which is probably what is happening in verse 13; the disciples treat the visit as an interruption of more important business. The word paidion covers children from infancy to about twelve, and Luke calls them infants (Luke 18:15).

Wealth was widely taken as a sign of God's favor, and Deuteronomy promises prosperity to the obedient (Deuteronomy 28:1-14), though the prophets and Proverbs also warn about riches gained by oppression. The disciples' astonishment in verses 24 and 26 is genuine: if the rich cannot enter, who can? The rich man's ‘great wealth’ (verse 22) was probably land (the Greek ktēmata often means estates), the most secure wealth a person could hold. Selling it meant ending a family's position. ‘Treasure in heaven’ was a Jewish expression for reward stored up with God through acts of mercy (compare Tobit 4:8-9). The camel and the needle's eye are a deliberate impossibility, the largest animal of the region and the smallest opening; the Babylonian Talmud uses an elephant passing through the eye of a needle for the same idea (b. Berakhot 55b). The suggestion that the needle was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall is not found in any ancient source and has no evidence behind it.

Sitting at a king's right and left meant the highest places of honor and power (1 Kings 2:19, Psalm 110:1). In the Old Testament the cup is a common image for the portion God pours out, often his judgment (Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15), and to be baptized, in ordinary Greek, could mean to be plunged or overwhelmed by disaster. A ransom (lutron) was the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner of war, or the payment by which a life forfeited under the law could be redeemed (Exodus 21:30). Blind people in the ancient world were usually reduced to begging, and Jericho's road, busy with pilgrims before Passover, was a good place for it. Bartimaeus's cloak was likely spread on the ground to collect alms and served as his covering at night; the law treated a poor man's cloak as something a creditor could not keep overnight (Exodus 22:26-27). Throwing it off meant leaving behind what little he had.
literary:
The chapter is built from encounters on the road, and each turns a common value upside down. Marriage is judged by creation rather than by what the law permits; children, not adults, show how the kingdom is received; a rich and righteous man is told he lacks one thing; the first will be last. Mark keeps his familiar pattern of public teaching followed by private explanation to the disciples ‘inside the house’ (verse 10; compare 4:10, 7:17, 9:28), and he repeats a gesture: Jesus looks around or looks at people before he speaks (verses 21, 23, 27).

The section 8:27 to 10:52 follows a threefold cycle: a prediction of the passion (8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34), a failure of the disciples to understand (8:32-33, 9:33-34, 10:35-41), and teaching on what following Jesus costs (8:34-38, 9:35-37, 10:42-45). This chapter brings the cycle to its height. Verses 32 to 34 give the fullest of the three predictions, with a chain of verbs (handed over, condemn, hand over, mock, spit on, flog, kill) followed by the promise that he will rise, and each item will return in the passion narrative. Verses 35 to 45 give the fullest misunderstanding and the fullest explanation. The whole section is also framed by the two healings of blind men (8:22-26 and 10:46-52), so that sight becomes a picture of understanding.

Mark links the scenes with repeated words. Jesus asks James and John and then Bartimaeus the same question, “What do you want Me to do for you?” (verses 36 and 51), and the two answers show the contrast Mark wants readers to see: disciples asking for glory, a beggar asking for sight. The rich man asks what he must do to ‘inherit’ eternal life (verse 17), and the disciples ask who can be ‘saved’ (verse 26); Jesus tells Bartimaeus that his faith has ‘saved’ him (the same verb, sōzō, translated “healed” in verse 52). The phrase ‘on the road’ (en tē hodō) opens and closes the section (8:27, 10:52), and the rich man who ‘went away’ (verse 22) is answered by the beggar who ‘followed Jesus along the road’. Jesus' words about children in verses 13 to 16 prepare for his address to the disciples as ‘children’ in verse 24, the only time he calls them this in Mark.

outline.t: Divorce and God's intent in creation
The rich man who went away sad
Wealth, the kingdom, and the reward of those who leave all
James and John ask for glory: the Son of Man came to serve

doctrines.note: Jesus grounds marriage in creation, joining Genesis 1:27 and 2:24: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh, so what God has joined no human should separate. Moses' provision for divorce was a regulation for hard hearts, not God's design. Jesus also makes the husband answerable to his wife (verse 11) and honors children as those to whom the kingdom belongs.

The rich man's possessions hold him back from following Jesus, and Jesus says it is harder for the rich to enter the kingdom than for a camel to pass through a needle's eye. Wealth is not condemned as such, but it is named as a rival master. Those who leave home and fields for Jesus' sake receive a new family and household now, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come.

The rich man asks what he must do, and the disciples ask who can be saved. Jesus answers that salvation is impossible for human beings and possible for God (verse 27). It is received as a child receives, not earned like an inheritance secured by performance, and Bartimaeus's cry for mercy shows the posture that receives it.

Verse 45 is Mark's clearest statement of why Jesus came: to give his life as a ransom for many. His death is a price paid to set others free, given in their place (anti, ‘in place of’). The word many echoes Isaiah 53:11-12, where the servant bears the sin of many, and the cup and baptism of verse 38 name the judgment he will undergo.

Jesus contrasts the rulers of the nations, who lord it over their subjects, with the way of his followers: the one who would be great must be a servant, and the one who would be first must be the slave of all. He grounds this not in a management principle but in his own death, which makes service the pattern of every office in his community.

words.note: Apoluō, to release or send away. It occurs about sixty-seven times in the New Testament, for releasing a prisoner (15:6), dismissing a crowd (6:45, 8:9), and, as here, a husband's sending away of his wife, the ordinary word for divorce. It appears four times in this chapter (verses 2, 4, 11, 12). BDAG lists divorce as one sense of a verb whose basic idea is setting free. The Pharisees ask whether a man may send his wife away; Jesus answers by asking what God has joined.

Sklērokardia, hardness of heart, a compound of hard and heart. It occurs three times in the New Testament (here, the parallel Matthew 19:8, and Mark 16:14 in the longer ending). The Greek Old Testament uses it in the call to circumcise the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16, Jeremiah 4:4). Jesus says Moses wrote the divorce regulation ‘for you’ because of it: a limit placed on a broken practice, not a statement of God's will.

Suzeugnumi, to yoke together, used of pairing animals under one yoke and, in Greek writers, of marriage. It occurs only here and in the parallel Matthew 19:6. The subject is God: marriage is not merely a contract two people make but a union God makes. The neuter relative (‘what’) makes the union itself the object that no human authority may undo.

Klēronomeō, to inherit. It occurs eighteen times in the New Testament, only here in Mark. In the Old Testament Israel ‘inherits’ the land as God's gift (Deuteronomy 4:1), and later Jewish writings speak of inheriting the age to come. The rich man's question, what must I do to inherit, mixes two ideas that do not fit, since an inheritance is received, not earned; Jesus answers with a child receiving the kingdom.

Diakoneō, to serve, originally to wait at table. It occurs thirty-seven times in the New Testament and five times in Mark: the angels serve Jesus (1:13), Peter's mother-in-law serves (1:31), the women who followed Jesus from Galilee served him (15:41), and here, twice, Jesus came not to be served but to serve (verse 45). The related noun diakonos, servant, in verse 43 later named an office in the church (Philippians 1:1). The Son of Man of Daniel 7 receives the service of all peoples; Jesus reverses the picture.

Lutron, ransom, the price paid to release a slave or captive or to redeem a forfeited life. It occurs only here and in the parallel Matthew 20:28, though related words are common (antilutron in 1 Timothy 2:6, lutroō in Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 1:18). In the Greek Old Testament it names the payment that redeems a firstborn or a life under the law (Exodus 21:30, Numbers 3:46-49). BDAG gives the sense price of release. Joined with anti, ‘in place of’, it describes Jesus' life given for others.

Potērion, cup. It occurs about thirty times in the New Testament and six times in Mark, among them a cup of water given in Jesus' name (9:41), the cup of this chapter (verses 38 and 39), the cup of the Last Supper (14:23), and the cup of Gethsemane, where Jesus prays that this cup be taken from him (14:36). The prophets used the cup for the portion God pours out, especially his wrath (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15), and Jesus takes it as a name for his coming suffering.

Eleeō, to have mercy, to show pity in action. It occurs about thirty times in the New Testament and three times in Mark (5:19, and twice here in verses 47 and 48). In the Greek Psalms it is the cry of the needy to God (Psalm 51:1). Bartimaeus's ‘have mercy on me’ became, with Luke 18:13, a root of the Kyrie eleison of Christian worship and of the Jesus Prayer of the Eastern churches.

christ:
This chapter shows who Jesus is by showing why he came. He speaks about marriage with an authority that goes behind Moses to what God intended ‘from the beginning of creation’ (verse 6), placing his own word alongside the Creator's. He welcomes children, whom his disciples turned away, and says the kingdom belongs to such as these. He looks at the rich man and loves him (verse 21), the only place in the first three Gospels where Jesus is said to love a particular person, and he makes following himself the one thing that man lacks, a claim no teacher of the law would make for himself. When the man calls him ‘Good Teacher’, Jesus answers that no one is good except God alone (verse 18). The saying does not deny his own goodness; it presses the man to consider what he has just said, and the rest of the scene, in which Jesus asks for what only God may ask, answers the question.

He is the Son of Man who goes up to Jerusalem knowing he will be handed over, mocked, flogged, and killed, and who will rise after three days. Mark pictures him walking ahead of the disciples on the road (verse 32), leading them toward his own death while they follow in fear. The title Son of Man comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives dominion and the service of all peoples. Jesus reverses the expectation: this Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and his service reaches its depth in giving his life ‘as a ransom for many’ (verse 45). The phrase gathers the language of Isaiah's servant, who pours out his life to death, is made a guilt offering, and bears the sin of many (Isaiah 53:10-12). Scholars debate how directly Mark's wording draws on Isaiah 53, but the idea of a life given in place of many is the heart of that chapter, and the New Testament everywhere reads Jesus' death that way. The cup and the baptism of verse 38 name the same death as the judgment God's servant undergoes for others, the cup he will ask to pass from him in Gethsemane (14:36).

The request of James and John for places at his right and left ‘in Your glory’ (verse 37) receives an answer Mark will make visible: when Jesus is enthroned as king, with the title ‘King of the Jews’ over his head, the men on his right and left are two robbers (15:27). The glory the brothers wanted is revealed on a cross.

Finally he is the Son of David, the title Bartimaeus shouts at Jericho, the first time anyone uses it of Jesus in Mark, just before Jesus enters David's city. Son of David named the royal Messiah promised in 2 Samuel 7:12-16, and some Jewish tradition also remembered David's son Solomon as a healer. Jesus stops for the man the crowd tried to silence, asks what he wants, and gives him sight, and the healed man follows him on the road that leads to the cross. The king who is about to be acclaimed in Jerusalem will reign by serving, and those who see him truly will follow him there.
interpretation:
Jesus' words on divorce have shaped Christian marriage law more than almost any other text. The Shepherd of Hermas (second century, Mandate 4.1) told a husband to put away an unrepentant adulterous wife but not to remarry, so that she could return if she repented. Augustine argued that the bond of marriage remains while both spouses live and that remarriage after divorce is adultery (On the Good of Marriage, about 401; On Adulterous Marriages, about 419), and the Western church followed him. The Council of Trent (Session 24, 1563) defended the Catholic teaching that the bond is not dissolved even by adultery, but worded its canon so as not to condemn the Eastern churches, which had long allowed remarriage in some cases. The Orthodox churches permit a second and, rarely, a third marriage by economy (oikonomia, pastoral dispensation), with a rite of penitential character. Erasmus, in his annotations on 1 Corinthians 7 (1519), argued that the innocent party might remarry, and the Reformers generally held that adultery and desertion dissolve a marriage; the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 24) permits divorce and remarriage for adultery or for desertion that cannot be remedied. Modern evangelical debate has included William Heth and Gordon Wenham (Jesus and Divorce, 1984), who argued that the early church allowed separation but not remarriage, and David Instone-Brewer (Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible, 2002), who read Jesus against the Hillel-Shammai debate and allowed wider grounds.

The blessing of the children became a text in the debate over infant baptism. Tertullian (On Baptism 18, about 200) used ‘do not forbid them’ to argue that children should come to baptism when they are old enough to know Christ. Calvin (Institutes 4.16.7) argued that if children may be brought to Christ, they should not be barred from baptism, the sign of fellowship with him. Luther's baptismal order (1526) and the 1549 Book of Common Prayer read Mark 10:13-16 at infant baptism, and Lucas Cranach and his workshop painted Christ Blessing the Children, from 1538, in more than twenty versions, a subject widely read as a Lutheran answer to the Anabaptists. Baptist and Anabaptist readers reply that the passage says nothing about baptism.

The rich man has been read in two directions. Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole treatise on Mark 10:17-31, Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, arguing that Jesus demands freedom from the love of wealth rather than its literal surrender. Athanasius tells how Antony of Egypt, hearing the parallel in Matthew 19:21 read in church, gave away his inherited land and went into the desert (Life of Antony 2), a scene that stands at the root of Christian monasticism. Heinrich Hofmann's painting Christ and the Rich Young Ruler (1889), now in the Riverside Church in New York, became one of the most widely reproduced images of the scene.

Verse 45 anchored early reflection on the atonement. Origen (Commentary on Matthew 16.8) held that the ransom was paid to the devil, who held humanity captive; Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 45.22) rejected the idea that the ransom was paid either to the evil one or, in the sense of a price demanded, to the Father. Anselm's Why God Became Man (1098), the Reformers' teaching on substitution, and Gustaf Aulén's Christus Victor (English 1931) all claimed the verse. Modern critical scholars have debated whether it goes back to Jesus (Rudolf Bultmann doubted it) and whether it draws on Isaiah 53 (C. K. Barrett and Morna Hooker doubted a direct link; Joachim Jeremias and Peter Stuhlmacher argued for it).

Bartimaeus's cry lives in liturgy as the Kyrie eleison and in the Jesus Prayer (‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me’), the prayer of the hesychast monks gathered in the Philokalia (1782). In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year B, the chapter is read on four autumn Sundays: verses 2 to 16 (Proper 22), 17 to 31 (Proper 23), 35 to 45 (Proper 24), and 46 to 52 (Proper 25).
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter, mostly where later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, smoothed a hard saying or harmonized Mark with Matthew and Luke.

Verse 1: the critical editions read ‘the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan’; most later manuscripts read ‘by the far side of the Jordan’, which the KJV follows. Verse 2: the words ‘Pharisees came’ are missing from some Western witnesses, including Codex Bezae, and the SBL Greek New Testament omits them; most versions keep them. Verse 7: the clause ‘and be united to his wife’ is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. Westcott and Hort omitted it, but most modern editions and English Bibles keep it, since a copyist's eye could skip from one ‘and’ to the next and verse 8's ‘the two’ needs it. Verse 12: manuscripts word the woman's act differently; the critical text has her divorce her husband, and some Western witnesses have her leave him, a form closer to Jewish practice.

Verse 21: the KJV's ‘take up the cross’ comes from later manuscripts and is absent from the earliest. Verse 24: the KJV's ‘for them that trust in riches’ is a later addition that turns a saying about the rich into one about attitude; it is absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. A few late manuscripts read kamilos, ‘rope’, for kamēlos, ‘camel’, in verse 25, another softening. Verse 29: the KJV adds ‘or wife’ to the list of what is left, from Luke 18:29. Verse 34: Mark's ‘after three days’ became ‘the third day’ in later manuscripts, matching Matthew and Luke; the two expressions meant the same thing in Jewish reckoning. Verse 43: where the critical text reads ‘it is not so among you’, many later manuscripts read ‘it shall not be so’, a command rather than a description.

The parallels differ too. Matthew adds ‘except for sexual immorality’ to the divorce saying (Matthew 19:9) and has the rich man ask ‘what good thing’ he must do (Matthew 19:16-17); Luke omits the divorce debate at this point. Matthew has two blind men at Jericho (Matthew 20:30) and Luke one, unnamed, as Jesus approaches the city (Luke 18:35).

teach.big: Jesus measures marriage, childhood, wealth, and power by the kingdom of God and grounds the new order in his own death: the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many, and those who see him follow him on that road.

outline.t: Jesus answers a trap about what the law permits by going back to what God intended: marriage is a union God makes, and the law's concession measures human hardness, not divine approval.
The kingdom belongs to those who can only receive it, and Jesus is angry when his followers keep the smallest and least useful away from him.
A sincere and moral man lacks the one thing that matters, because his possessions hold the place that belongs to following Jesus; Jesus loves him and still asks for everything.
Wealth makes entering the kingdom humanly impossible, and so does every other form of self-reliance; salvation is God's work where human ability ends.
Nothing given up for Jesus and the gospel is lost: those who leave receive a new family now, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come, in a kingdom where the first are last.
Jesus walks ahead toward his death, knowing every stage of it in advance and promising his resurrection; he goes to the cross, he is not dragged.
Even the closest disciples want glory without the cup, and their anger at each other shows the same ambition.
In Jesus' community greatness is service, because the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom in the place of many.
A blind beggar sees what the disciples have missed: he calls Jesus Son of David, asks for mercy, receives sight, and follows him on the road to Jerusalem.

teach.pitfalls:
The divorce passage is often taught either as a rulebook that ignores the rest of the New Testament or as an ideal so distant that it asks nothing. Mark gives Jesus' teaching in its sharpest form, and Matthew and Paul show the church applying it to cases Mark does not address (Matthew 19:9, 1 Corinthians 7:15). Teach the saying in its strength and in its setting: it answered men who could dismiss a wife at will, and it protected the one with no power to divorce. Do not use it to shame people who have been divorced, many of whom did not choose it.

Verses 13 to 16 are sometimes reduced to a lesson about childlike innocence. Children in the ancient world were not symbols of purity but of dependence and low status; the point is receiving, not being sweet. Verses 17 to 27 are misused in two opposite ways: by explaining the camel away (the needle gate or the rope) so that the rich are comfortable, or by teaching that the saying applies only to this one man. Jesus' command to this man was particular, but the warning in verses 23 to 25 is addressed to the disciples and generalized in verse 24. Verses 29 and 30 have been used by prosperity teachers to promise a hundredfold return on gifts; Mark's ‘along with persecutions’ and the new family of the church answer that reading.

Verse 45 should not be flattened into a lesson on servant leadership detached from the atonement, nor into a doctrine of the atonement detached from service; Jesus joins the two. Finally, avoid making James and John into villains while the rest of the class stands outside; the ten were angry because they wanted the same thing.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on the divorced, the remarried, children of divorce, and people in hard or dangerous marriages. Teach with care. Say plainly that Jesus spoke to men who could send a wife away at will, and that his words defended the one with no power to leave. Do not imply that everyone divorced chose it: many were abandoned or betrayed, and verse 11 names the husband who divorces as the one who wrongs his wife. Christians differ on remarriage: the Catholic Church holds a valid sacramental marriage indissoluble while caring for the innocent party and examining claims of nullity, the Orthodox churches permit a second marriage in penitence by economy, and most Protestant churches allow divorce and remarriage after adultery or desertion, many also after abuse. Name these fairly and let people follow their own church's counsel. Jesus' words never require anyone to remain where they or their children are in danger; separation for safety is not the sin this text condemns. Anyone facing abuse should seek safety first and help from their church and from qualified professionals; this note is not legal advice. The rich man's story also presses on scrupulous consciences; Jesus looked at him and loved him before he asked anything.

hard.q: Does Jesus' teaching on divorce mean that divorce and remarriage are never permitted?
hard.a:
The objection comes in several forms. Historical critics note that Mark gives the saying without exception, that Matthew adds ‘except for sexual immorality’ (Matthew 5:32, 19:9), and that Paul adds the case of desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15). John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 4, 2009) concludes that the historical Jesus forbade divorce outright and that the exceptions show the early church adapting a demand it found too hard; skeptical readers take this as evidence that the church has always softened Jesus when it needed to. Jewish readers raise a different objection: the Torah itself regulates divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1-4), and to call remarriage after a lawful divorce adultery seems to set Jesus against Moses. Rabbinic tradition also grieved divorce (b. Gittin 90b) but never forbade it, since a marriage that has died can be a prison. Others ask how a teaching that seems to bind the abused to their abusers can be good.

Christians have answered in different ways, and the positions are held by serious readers in every tradition. The Catholic Church teaches that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power while both spouses live (Council of Trent, Session 24; Catechism of the Catholic Church 2382-2386). It permits separation, distinguishes the innocent victim of a civil divorce from the one who caused it, and examines whether a true marriage existed in the first place (a declaration of nullity). The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be lifelong in intent but, following an old Eastern practice, allow a second and even a third marriage by economy, with a penitential rite, as a mercy to people whose first marriage has died. Most Protestant churches, following Erasmus and the Reformers, read Matthew's exception and Paul's words as showing that adultery and desertion break the marriage covenant and free the innocent party to remarry (Westminster Confession 24.5-6); many now include abuse as a form of desertion or covenant-breaking. Some evangelical scholars, including Heth and Wenham (Jesus and Divorce, 1984), argue that Jesus allowed separation but not remarriage, as the early church largely held; Instone-Brewer (2002) argues that Jesus rejected the Hillelite ‘any cause’ divorce while assuming the grounds of Exodus 21:10-11.

To the Jewish objection, Christian readers reply that Jesus does not deny that Moses wrote the law but reads it as a limit on hard hearts, and appeals from Deuteronomy to Genesis, as the Damascus Document also did. All these views share Jesus' main point: God designed marriage as a lifelong union, and divorce is always a tearing of what he joined, never a neutral legal option. This note is not legal advice; anyone facing separation or abuse should seek help from their church and from qualified professionals.

hard.q: What does it mean that Jesus gave his life as a ransom, and to whom was it paid?
hard.a:
The strongest objections come from two sides. Historical critics ask whether Jesus said it. Rudolf Bultmann regarded the ransom clause as a later formulation of the church's theology, and C. K. Barrett and Morna Hooker (Jesus and the Servant, 1959) argued that the wording does not depend on Isaiah 53, since lutron never appears there. Moral critics object to the idea itself: if God requires a death before he forgives, he seems less loving than a human father who simply forgives. Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker (For God So Loved the World?, 1989) argued that the cross as a saving death glorifies suffering and makes God an abuser, and many Jewish readers have objected that the Hebrew Bible teaches repentance, not a substitute's death, as the way back to God (Ezekiel 18:21-22). The ancient question ‘paid to whom?’ adds a puzzle: a ransom paid to the devil gives evil rights over God, while a ransom paid to God seems to set the Father against the Son.

Responses begin with the text. Joachim Jeremias, Peter Stuhlmacher, and Rikki Watts argue that the idea of a life given in place of many, as a payment that releases them, is exactly what Isaiah 53:10-12 says of the servant, whose life is made a guilt offering and who bears the sin of many, even if Mark does not quote the Greek. Jewish tradition itself could speak of the deaths of the righteous as atoning for Israel (4 Maccabees 6:28-29, 17:22). The church fathers answered the ‘to whom’ question in different ways: Origen spoke of a ransom paid to the devil; Gregory of Nazianzus rejected that and denied that the Father demanded the price, saying the Father accepted the offering because of his plan for humanity. Anselm (Why God Became Man, 1098) and the Reformers read the ransom as satisfaction of God's justice by God himself in the Son; Gustaf Aulén (Christus Victor, 1931) read it as the liberation of captives from the powers of sin and death. Many theologians hold that ransom is a picture of cost and liberation, not a transaction with a receiver to be named, and they answer the moral objection by stressing that in the cross God does not punish a reluctant third party but gives himself: the Son ‘came’ to give his life. Mark's own emphasis is on the giver: the one who could have been served chose to serve, and his life freed many.

observe: Jesus asks what Moses ‘commanded’, and the Pharisees answer with what Moses ‘permitted’ (verses 3 and 4). Where does Jesus take the discussion next, and why?
Compare what the rich man asks (verse 17) with what Bartimaeus asks (verse 51). What does each man call Jesus, and how does each respond at the end?
List every stage of the third passion prediction (verses 33 and 34). Which of them can you trace later in Mark's passion narrative?
interpret: Why does Jesus say the kingdom must be received ‘like a little child’, and how does that saying prepare for the story of the rich man?
What do the cup and the baptism of verse 38 mean, and why does Jesus say the brothers will share them?
How does verse 45 explain both why Jesus' followers should serve and why Jesus must die?
apply: Jesus looked at the rich man and loved him before asking him to give everything up. What holds the place in your life that belongs to following him?
Where in your family, church, or work are you seeking the seat at the right hand, and what would it look like to serve there instead?
If Jesus asked you, “What do you want Me to do for you?” what would you honestly say, and would it be closer to the brothers' request or to Bartimaeus's?
